passages.text: The harbour was quiet that morning. A thin mist lay over the water, and the gulls had not yet begun their arguments. Margaret walked along the sea wall with her hands in her pockets, counting the boats as she had done since she was a child. Most of them were still tied up, their ropes creaking softly. Only the old ferry was moving, a dark shape sliding out towards the islands. She stopped by the lighthouse and watched it go, wondering, not for the first time, what it would be like to leave.

A PDF file is built from objects: dictionaries, arrays, strings, numbers and streams. The cross-reference table at the end of the file records where each object begins, so a reader can jump straight to the page it needs. When a document is edited, the changes are usually appended as an incremental update rather than rewriting the whole file. This keeps earlier digital signatures valid, because the bytes they cover never change. Tagged documents add a structure tree that describes headings, paragraphs, lists and tables in their logical order, which assistive technology uses to read the content sensibly.

Reading for a long time should feel restful. The voice must not drift louder or quieter as the minutes pass, and the pauses between sentences should stay even. Short sentences help. So do clear breaks between paragraphs. A listener who loses their place should be able to find it again without effort. The garden behind the library had been neglected for years. Brambles covered the old brick paths, and the fountain had long since stopped. Every spring, though, the tulips came back, red and yellow among the weeds. The librarian, a patient man called Thomas, began to clear a corner each Saturday morning. He started with the bench under the apple tree. Then he found the sundial, its numbers worn almost smooth. By midsummer the path to the fountain was open again. Children from the reading group came out to help him. They pulled weeds, carried stones and argued about where the herbs should go. Nobody remembered who had planted the garden in the first place. There were rumours, of course: a retired sea captain, a botanist, a pair of sisters who ran the school. Thomas preferred not to choose. He liked the idea that it belonged to everyone. In the autumn the council noticed and offered a small grant. It paid for a new pump, some tools and a sign by the gate. The sign simply said that the garden was open to all, from dawn until dusk. Visitors began to bring books outside on warm afternoons. Some read quietly; others read aloud to friends. The sound of turning pages mixed with birdsong and the trickle of the fountain. It was, Thomas thought, exactly what a library should be. When winter came, the garden rested. The paths stayed clear, and the bench was swept after every frost. In the new year the children planted bulbs along the wall. They wrote their names on little wooden labels so they would know which flowers were theirs. Spring, when it arrived, was early and generous. The tulips returned, joined now by daffodils and a ragged line of crocuses. Thomas sat on the bench with a cup of tea and watched the first visitors arrive. He did not say much. He did not need to.
